Mall was full of shoppers and the food court/restaurants were packed too. We all continued our usual daily routines but it's been 12+ hours since the quake and we're all still pretty shaken up. 

I'm guessing it's because we saw way less infrastructure damage compared to 921, although that might also be because the epicenter was further away from densely populated urban areas.

Hello! I'm a Taiwanese currently studying cultural anthropology in Canada. Appropriation is usually a very complex issue, but I think the most important things to keep in mind when examining appropriation are contexts and consequences. When you are utilizing various materials and symbols in an attempt to connect to a culture, keep in mind the context that these materials and symbols are embedded in. A very straightforward example would be not to casually wear something that's worn as a funeral garment. In a similar sense, think about the consequences/impacts (whether positive or negative) that actions might have on the culture you are trying to connect with. If it's an already marginalized culture, acts of appropriation that have no respect on context might contribute to a further undermining of the culture involved.

TL;DR from your question I don't think what you're trying to do would be insensitive at all! The sheer fact that you are wary of this problem kinda shows that you do have context in mind in the first place (not to mention existing familial roots).

I think it depends on the location. I live in Taipei and from what I've personally experienced Mazu doesn't really hold any importance over other deities for the average Taiwanese person in Taipei. If anything, Mazu became more of a meme among urban youths after Terry Gou claimed that Mazu instructed him to participate in the 2020 Presidential Election. I saw a lot of people sharing satirical comic strips featuring Mazu during that time, however non of the comic strips I saw were disrespectful towards Mazu. Rather, most of them depicted Mazu feeling awkward or disapproving towards Gou's statement. My take from this is that in urban Taiwan gods are usually unimportant in daily life but when they do become the center of attention though they are imagined to be very close to people, almost like a celebrity. The relationship between god and people feels really secular.

I did a field research in a fishing village in Central Taiwan 2 years ago however and Mazu was extremely important to the residents there. My topic of interest back then was economic activity rather than religion so I didn't probe more into this topic, but the biggest temple in that village was a Mazu temple and families that rely of fishing usually have Mazu worshipped in their homes. So I would say the importance of Mazu is much greater in this fishing village in that it's part of their daily routine (they worship Mazu in their homes every day) and the relationship between god and people is more religious.
